extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate or beginning_graduate students studying real analysis (working through Rudin-style exercises)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of advanced undergraduate/introductory graduate real-analysis exercise prompts (Riemann–Stieltjes integration, vector-valued integration, rectifiable curves, sequences/series of functions, uniform convergence) intended to be solved/proved by students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of F(x)=∫_a^x f dα for f ∈ (α)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ (α) and F(x) = ∫_{t=a}^x f(t) dα(t), then (i) F(a)=0; (ii) for all x1,x2 with a ≤ x1 < x2 ≤ b, ΔF ∈ [(Δα)(inf f(x)), (Δα)(sup f(x))], where the inf and sup are over x∈[x1,x2].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may write conclusion more suggestively as ΔF/Δα ∈ [inf f, sup f], but note Δα might be zero. This is the basic estimate relating increments of the integral-function to increments of α and extremal values of f on subintervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of an antiderivative-like function for Riemann–Stieltjes integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that F is the unique function satisfying (i) F(a)=0 and (ii) ΔF ∈ [(Δα)(inf f), (Δα)(sup f)] for all subintervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bounds in (ii) to force any two such functions to coincide (consider upper and lower integrals and show inequalities force equality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: existence of unique F implies f ∈ (α)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if there is a unique function F on [a,b] satisfying the conditions (i) and (ii) above, then the bounded function f on [a,b] belongs to (α) (i.e., is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable with respect to α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the upper and lower integral-functions F^+(x)=∫_a^x f dα (upper) and F^–(x)=∫_a^x f dα (lower); show they satisfy the conditions and hence squeeze any F between them, forcing equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-variables identity for nested integrals (6.6:7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose α is monotone increasing on [a,b] and f,g are continuous on [a,b] with g nonnegative. Prove that ∫_{t=a}^x f(t) ( ∫_{s=a}^t g(s) dα(s) ) dt = ∫_{t=a}^x f(t) g(t) dα(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint in text: first prove the case when u and v (or here g) are nonnegative-valued using part (a). This is a change-of-variables / Fubini-style rearrangement for the Stieltjes integral under continuity and nonnegativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability of vector-valued functions via partition diameter sums (6.7:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f:[a,b]→R^k and α:[a,b]→R increasing. f is integrable with respect to α iff for every ε>0 there exists a partition P={x0,...,xn} of [a,b] such that Σ_{i=1}^n diam(f([x_{i-1},x_i])) Δα_i < ε, where 'diam' denotes the diameter of a set and Δα_i = α(x_i)-α(x_{i-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (b),(c) refine this: for such a partition P any choice of tags ti gives Riemann–Stieltjes sums close to the integral (difference < ε), and any refinement of P also satisfies the inequality. Use these to control vector-valued integrals via uniform smallness of image diameters weighted by α-increments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Stieltjes sums approximation for vector-valued integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f integrable w.r.t α and a partition P as above, for every choice of points ti∈[x_{i-1},x_i], we have |Σ_{i=1}^n f(ti) Δα_i – ∫_a^b f dα| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the quantitative approximation guarantee coming from the diameter-weighted partition condition; choose partition to make total variation of f on each subinterval small relative to α-increments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement stability of integrability condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Every refinement P* of a partition P that satisfies Σ diam(f([x_{i-1},x_i])) Δα_i < ε also satisfies the same inequality (hence refinements preserve the integrability condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monotonicity of α and subadditivity of diameters over subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectifiability implies differentiability? (exercise prompt)
rubrics_metrics.description: True/false style prompt: If γ is a rectifiable curve in R^k, then γ is differentiable and γ' is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is to be judged/proved; the text raises such T/F questions to test understanding—consider known counterexamples: rectifiable need not imply differentiable everywhere or continuous derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space-filling curves cannot be rectifiable (6.8:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a curve in R^2 whose image is the whole unit square [0,1]^2 cannot be rectifiable (i.e., cannot have finite length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approach: find c such that any curve containing a solid square of side s must have a subcurve of length ≥ c s in the interior; subdivide into n^2 small squares and let n→∞ to force arbitrarily large length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound on length for curves filling a neighborhood (busy-body curves) (6.8:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every positive constant C there exists ε>0 such that any curve in R^2 whose image has points at distance ≤ ε from each point of the unit square [0,1]^2 must have length ≥ C. Use this to derive the previous exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use covering/subdivision arguments; this is a quantitative strengthening of non-rectifiability for space-filling-like images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability of γ' suffices for curve-length formula (6.8:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ:[a,b]→R^k is differentiable and γ'∈L^1 (integrable), then the usual curve-length formula Λ(γ)=∫_a^b |γ'(t)| dt holds; exercise asks to show approximations of sums by integrals given partitions making diameter-weighted sums small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the integrability of γ' to control differences |γ(x_i)-γ(x_{i-1})| and compare Riemann sums of |γ'| with polygonal lengths; the earlier vector-valued integrability exercise is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence definitions of double limit lim_{m,n→∞} s_{m,n} = p (7.1:2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show equivalence of: (i) For every ε>0 there exist M,N such that for all m≥M and n≥N, d(s_{m,n},p) < ε; and (ii) For every ε>0 there exists N such that for all m≥N and n≥N, d(s_{m,n},p) < ε. When equivalent we write lim_{m,n→∞} s_{m,n} = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes joint convergence in two indices. Use definitions carefully to show the two quantifier patterns are equivalent for double limits as defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated limits imply joint limit (7.1:2(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{m,n→∞} s_{m,n} = p then lim_{m→∞} lim_{n→∞} s_{m,n} also exists and equals p (when the inner iterated limits exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the joint ε–N condition to pass to iterated limits; note converse need not hold in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal selection for iterated limits (7.1:3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for each m the limit lim_{n→∞} s_{m,n} exists and lim_{m→∞} lim_{n→∞} s_{m,n} = p, then there exists a sequence of positive integers n_m (with n_m ≥ N_m chosen suitably) such that lim_{m→∞} s_{m,n_m} = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct N_m so that tail terms are within 1/m of their limit and choose n_m ≥ N_m to form diagonal sequence; standard diagonal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: '1 on rationals' function not a pointwise limit of continuous functions (7.1:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the function f:R→{0,1} equal to 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals is not itself a pointwise limit of any sequence (f_n) of continuous functions R→R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use density of rationals/irrationals and Baire/category or pointwise behavior arguments; Rudin's earlier exercise shows it's a pointwise limit of pointwise limits but not of a single sequence of continuous functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone sequence of continuous functions on compact K ⇒ uniform convergence (Dini-type) (7.3:0(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) is a sequence of continuous real-valued functions on a compact metric space K with f_n(x) ≤ f_{n+1}(x) for all x and n, and f_n → f pointwise where f is continuous, then f_n → f uniformly on K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Dini's theorem; use compactness to upgrade monotone pointwise convergence of continuous functions to uniform convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence preserves algebraic operations under boundedness (7:R2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) and (g_n) converge uniformly to f and g respectively, then f_n+g_n → f+g uniformly; product likewise if the sequences are uniformly bounded (exception: product may fail if unbounded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard ε–N estimates; watch for the boundedness hypothesis in the product case.

rubrics_metrics.name: On finite sets uniform and pointwise convergence coincide (7.2:1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E is a finite set and (f_n) are functions E→C, then (f_n) converges pointwise iff it converges uniformly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite maxima reduce pointwise to uniform; also every subsequence of a uniformly convergent sequence converges uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence and continuity: uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous on compact domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.13 (continuous functions on a compact K converging uniformly), the limit is continuous; several exercises probe necessity of hypotheses and variants (e.g., local uniform convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask for counterexamples if hypotheses are dropped and suggest methods (use Theorem 7.13 or adapt its proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence equivalent to convergence in sup-norm metric; bounded variant for all functions (7.3:11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform convergence on a set E is convergence in the metric ||f-g||_∞. For unbounded functions, define d(f,g)=min(||f-g||_∞,1) to obtain a metric where uniform convergence ↔ convergence in d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note this metric loses some linear-scaling properties (d(c f, c g) ≠ c d(f,g) in general), but is useful to treat all functions in a single metric framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointwise convergence is not convergence in any metric (7.3:12 & 7.3:17 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct families g_{m,n} of continuous functions on [0,1] with the property that for each fixed m, g_{m,n}→0 pointwise as n→∞, but there is no diagonal subsequence n_m making g_{m,n_m}→0; deduce no metric on C([0,1]) can have convergence equivalent to pointwise convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constructions given: one using previously constructed sequences (7.3:12) and a self-contained binary expansion construction (7.3:17). These exhibit failure of metric convergence property in 7.1:3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence as uniform continuity on a product space (7.3:15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S={1/n}∪{0}, X=E×S with metric product-type; define F((p,1/n))=f_n(p), F((p,0))=f(p). Then f_n→f pointwise iff F is continuous; f_n→f uniformly iff F is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise provides a geometric/topological view of uniform convergence; verify metric properties and equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform continuity characterized by uniform convergence constructions (7.3:16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given F:X→C, construct sequences on X×X or related spaces so that pointwise/uniform convergence of these sequences corresponds to continuity/uniform continuity of F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constructions are given: one simpler (possibly 'hokey') and one more natural but more complex. Use these to relate uniform continuity to uniform convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally uniform convergence: definition and basic implications (7.3:19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define (f_n)→f locally uniformly if for every x∈X and ε>0 there exists δ>0 and N such that for n≥N and d(x,y)<δ we have |f_n(y)-f(y)|≤ε. Uniform ⇒ locally uniform ⇒ pointwise. On compact spaces, locally uniform ⇔ uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask for examples showing none of the implications is reversible in general and derive variants of Theorem 7.13 using locally uniform convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and (locally) uniform convergence (7.3:20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n→f locally uniformly on Y and m:X→Y is continuous, then f_n∘m→f∘m locally uniformly. If m is uniformly continuous stronger conclusions obtain; counterexamples show plain uniform continuity of m is needed to preserve (global) uniform convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (b) asks for a counterexample if 'locally' is deleted; part (c) shows uniform continuity of m restores the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformly convergent sequence of uniformly continuous functions is uniformly continuous (7.3:18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) are uniformly continuous functions on a metric space X and f_n→f uniformly, then f is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straightforward triangle-inequality/ε–N proof; use uniform continuity of each f_n and uniform closeness to f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence on compact sets from series of nonnegative continuous functions (7.3:4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) is a sequence of nonnegative-valued continuous functions on a compact metric space K and the series Σ f_n converges pointwise to a continuous function, then the series converges uniformly on K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monotone convergence properties and Dini-type or Weierstrass M-test style arguments adapted to nonnegative monotone partial sums and compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence preserves restriction/uniformity behavior (7.2:0(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence (f_n) converges uniformly on X and E⊆X, then the restrictions f_n|_E also converge uniformly on E. The converse (uniform convergence on a subset implies uniform convergence on the whole set) is false in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counterexamples for the converse; the forward implication is immediate by restriction of suprema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence and subsequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If (f_n) converges uniformly then every subsequence (f_{n_k}) also converges uniformly to the same limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence gives an N independent of index so same N works for subsequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence and polynomial approximation examples (7.3:1 and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples showing uniform limits of polynomials: from probability/polynomial sequences p_n(t) one can get uniform convergence to functions like t p_∞(t) on [0,1], and deduce uniform approximation results including approximation of |·| on compact intervals by polynomials (Weierstrass-like constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises guide you through constructing uniform approximations via limits of polynomials, change of variables, and algebraic manipulations (subtracting constants to make polynomials vanish at 0, etc.).
